name: Interview English
lede: Walk in ready to talk about your work — the impact you’ve had, the decisions you owned, and what you want next. These words make a career story sound clear, specific, and true.
outcome: Tell a clear career story: the impact you made, the ownership you took, and the role you want next.
outcomes: Describe your impact with numbers, not adjectives, and keep the story under two minutes.
Answer behavioural questions with a clear situation, the action you took, and the result.
Ask questions back that show you understand the role, the team, and the risk.

aside.title: You already have the stories.
aside.body: This pack gives you the words to tell them clearly, without sounding rehearsed or over-polished.

words.definition: The clear difference your work made for a team or business.
words.example: The biggest impact was cutting onboarding time from six weeks to two.

words.definition: Taking full responsibility for a problem and seeing it through.
words.example: I took ownership of the backlog and cleared it in a quarter.

words.definition: Your history of achieving results over a period of time.
words.example: I’ve got a track record of turning around struggling teams.

words.definition: Covering a whole process from its first step to the last.
words.example: I owned the end-to-end launch, from research through to support.

words.definition: Involving people from several teams with different skills and goals.
words.example: I led a cross-functional group of product, sales, and support staff.

words.definition: To push a project or result forward with energy and focus.
words.example: I drove the migration and kept every team on schedule.

words.definition: Directly involved in the work rather than only managing it.
words.example: I stayed hands-on with the code during the first release.

words.definition: Focused on long-term goals rather than daily tasks.
words.example: I set the strategic direction, then let the team own delivery.

words.definition: A new project or plan you start yourself.
words.example: I started a mentoring initiative that cut new-hire turnover by half.

words.definition: To be the person who guides a piece of work.
words.example: I took the lead on the pricing review when it stalled.

words.definition: The result that came from your work or decision.
words.example: The outcome was a 20% rise in renewals within six months.

words.definition: The numbers you use to judge whether something worked.
words.example: We agreed on three metrics before the pilot started.

words.definition: Able to be counted or proved with clear evidence.
words.example: Every goal I set has a measurable target attached.

words.definition: A major improvement in a business or team that was failing.
words.example: The turnaround took eighteen months and began with clearer priorities.

words.definition: To grow a team, process, or product without losing quality.
words.example: I scaled the support team from four people to thirty.

words.definition: To introduce a new product or service to the market.
words.example: We launched the app in three markets on the same day.

words.definition: To release finished work to customers, often after testing.
words.example: We shipped the new checkout flow two weeks ahead of plan.

words.definition: A plan showing what you will build and in what order.
words.example: I rebuilt the roadmap around three customer problems, not features.

words.definition: To decide which tasks matter most and do them first.
words.example: I prioritise work by revenue risk, not by who shouts loudest.

words.definition: A situation where the next step is not yet clear.
words.example: I’m comfortable with ambiguity, but I still set a direction.

words.definition: The freedom to decide how you do your work.
words.example: I was given autonomy to rebuild the process my own way.

words.definition: Regularly helping someone with less experience to develop.
words.example: Mentoring two juniors into team leads was my proudest result.

words.definition: A move to a more senior role in the same organisation.
words.example: I earned a promotion after leading the platform rebuild.

words.definition: The time you must keep working after resigning from a job.
words.example: My notice period is four weeks, and I can start in May.

words.definition: The salary and benefits you receive for doing a job.
words.example: I’m looking at the whole package, not just base compensation.

words.definition: A trial period at the start of a new job.
words.example: The role starts with a three-month probation, which suits me.

words.definition: Something you do particularly well in your work.
words.example: My strength is turning vague briefs into clear, shippable plans.

words.definition: Something you find difficult and are still working to improve.
words.example: My weakness is saying yes to too many small requests.

words.definition: The sequence of roles you want to move through over time.
words.example: My career path has moved from analysis into product leadership.

words.definition: The area of work and decisions you are responsible for.
words.example: My remit grew to include pricing, packaging, and partnerships.
